Basic Space (blackbox) scaling

Source: R/svt.R
bbscal.Rd

Recovers respondents' positions from a respondent-by-issue matrix of responses by the decomposition of Poole (1998), \(X_0 = \Psi W' + J_n c' + E_0\) over the observed cells. Each dimension starts from the sign-corrected respondent means (column polarities from the pairwise correlations) and is refined by four alternating least-squares sweeps on the residuals of the earlier dimensions; up to five joint sweeps follow, stopping once the two half-step error sums of squares differ by less than 0.01; the fitted \(\Psi W'\) is then re-expressed by its singular value decomposition, \(\Psi = U D^{1/2}\), \(W = V D^{1/2}\). Respondents with fewer than minscale responses are not scaled. The sign of each dimension is arbitrary.

Usage

bbscal(X, ndim = 2, minscale = 8)

Arguments

X

A respondent-by-issue matrix of responses, NA for missing.

ndim

The number of dimensions (at most one fewer than the issues and than the scaled respondents).

minscale

The fewest responses a respondent needs to be scaled (capped at the number of issues).

Value

A list of class bbscal: ideal (respondents by dimensions, NA rows for those not scaled), weights (issues by dimensions), eigen and singular (of the fitted \(\Psi W'\)), fit (\(1 - SSE/SS\), SS about the grand mean of the observed cells), cmeans (the issue intercepts \(c\)) and ndim.

References

Poole, K. T. (1998). Recovering a basic space from a set of issue scales. American Journal of Political Science, 42(3), 954-993. doi:10.2307/2991737

See also

Other scaling: amscal(), anchv(), anomin(), bamscl(), bmdsf(), bunfld(), cjrirt(), cmdsf(), cutlns(), dblctr(), dwnom(), dynirt(), indscl(), ipsrec(), irtem(), irtlik(), irtpst(), mdsfit(), mlsmu(), nmdsf(), nombt(), nomll(), nompr(), nomutl(), nrmvec(), optcls(), ordirt(), ordocl(), procrs(), scboot(), smacf(), smunf(), unfstr(), votagr(), wrdfsh()

Examples

# 30 simulated respondents on eight issues, ten answers missing
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(60), 30, 2) %*% matrix(rnorm(16), 2, 8) +
  matrix(rnorm(240, 0, 0.3), 30, 8)
X[sample(240, 10)] <- NA
bbscal(X, ndim = 2)$fit
#> [1] 0.9787813
